title: Prefill-Decode Timeslice Orchestrator and Kernel Reuse Policy
creator: Marcus Lee
description:
Goal: Reduce 95th/99th tail latency for mixed short/long sequence workloads by coordinating prefill and decode scheduling across kernel selection boundaries, introducing time-sliced admission windows (timeslices) and a kernel reuse policy that prefers cached-compatibility to avoid kernel warmups.

Background: We frequently see microbursts of short requests triggering kernel switches for long-context models; the resulting kernel load/unload and attention memory pattern mismatches increase tail latency. Existing admission control operates at request-level and batch-shape level but does not account for tight prefill->decode handoffs and kernel compilation/selection costs. This ticket designs an orchestrator that schedules admission into small timeslices, maintains a short-lived kernel affinity window to reuse already-selected kernels for subsequent prefill/decode, and shapes batches to reduce kernel churn while keeping latency SLOs.

Design summary:
- Timeslice admission controller: group incoming requests into 5-20ms timeslices based on request arrival patterns and SLO class; allow priority fast-path exempting some low-token short requests.
- Kernel affinity window: maintain per-device short TTL (e.g., 100-500ms) where a selected kernel remains preferred for new prefill/decodes that are compatible; fallback to alternate kernels if slot pressure is high.
- Prefill/Decode synchronizer: prefer co-locating prefill and decode phases for a request within the same timeslice and kernel window to enable KV cache reuse and eliminate edge warmups.
- Batch shaping heuristics: adaptive early-cutoff for long sequences to limit batch width in timeslices when a single long-prefill would otherwise block kernel reuse.
- Metrics + safety: enforce per-tenant SLO budget, circuit-break on error spikes, and telemetry for kernel switch rate, median/95/99 latencies prefill vs decode, and KV cache hit ratio.

Acceptance criteria:
- 95th latency improvement >= 15% on mixed workload benchmark (short 60% / long 40% token mix) compared to baseline runtime-1.23 config.
- Kernel switch rate decreased by >= 30% during synthetic microburst tests.
- No regression in median latency > 5% for short-tail fast-path requests.
- Automated e2e benchmark in CI that simulates timeslices to validate metrics.

Implementation plan:
1) Prototype admission timeslices in a feature-flagged runtime gate; expose config: timeslice_ms, affinity_ttl_ms, fast_path_threshold_tokens.
2) Implement per-device kernel affinity cache and integration with kernel selector so selector can prefer affinity matches with a small penalty factor.
3) Add prefill->decode synchronizer that signals decode stage to prefer local KV cache if within affinity window.
4) Integrate batch-shaper heuristics into admission logic; tune via staged experiments.
5) Telemetry: add kernel_switch_count, kernel_affinity_hit, timeslice_utilization, per-tenant SLO burn rate to console dashboards.
6) Canary rollout: capacity-limited rollout to dedicated pool with canary telemetry alerts and automatic rollback if tail rises.

Testing & benchmarks:
- Unit tests for timeslice bucketing and affinity TTL behaviors.
- Integration tests that simulate mixed workloads with realistic inter-arrival distributions (Poisson + bursts).
- Hardware-in-loop tests on cheap GPU pool mirroring production model and kernel set.
- Benchmark scripts and dashboards to compare runtime-1.23 vs this feature. Use the 'mixed-workload-regen' harness in infra repo.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- TTL sizing vs responsiveness: longer affinity TTL reduces kernel churn but may hurt fairness for other workloads; test with adaptive TTL that shortens under contention.
- Fast-path exemptions risk starving reuse benefits; we must ensure median regressions for exempted classes are monitored.
- Quantization/kernel variants compatibility: when affinity prefers a kernel but request requires a different quantized path, we should fallback quickly; need defined penalty heuristics.

Risks & mitigations:
- Increased complexity in admission logic may introduce regressions; mitigate via feature flag + heavy canarying.
- Observability gaps: ensure telemetry is high-cardinality enough to attribute regressions to kernel affinity decisions.

Deliverables:
- RFC doc linked in comments (Confluence): runtime/ENG-482721-rfc
- Feature-flagged runtime implementation + unit/integration tests
- CI benchmark job and console dashboard tiles
- Rollout playbook and rollback criteria
